title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Data is not neutral
It’s tempting to think of data as raw facts which exist before anyone looks at them. But all data was collected by someone, for some purpose, and someone decided what was worth counting - and what wasn’t.
Collecting data has always been a source of power. When Thomas Paine published Common Sense in 1776, arguing for American independence, he included a table estimating the cost of building a navy, ship by ship. The table was there to persuade: it made independence look not only right, but affordable. Governments count their populations to tax them, conscript them, and decide who belongs. Many of the historical datasets you might use for your reports were collected by states, companies, or colonial administrations, for their own purposes - not for yours.
This means that you should always ask:
crumbs: Week 5 · Tue 24 Nov: Ethics, FAIR Data & Accessibility

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Who collected this data, and why?
What did they choose to record, and what did they leave out?
Who is in the data, and who is missing?
crumbs: Week 5 · Tue 24 Nov: Ethics, FAIR Data & Accessibility

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Visualisations are not neutral either
Charts can feel even more objective than tables. A clean chart with a straight axis and a source line at the bottom looks like a simple picture of ‘what is’. The humanities scholar Johanna Drucker has argued that this is exactly the problem: visualisations are so persuasive that they’re often taken to be simply a presentation of “what is”, and we forget that someone made them.
Every chart is an argument. Think about the choices you’ve made in the earlier chapters:

What to include. Filtering to one country, one period, or one category tells a different story to the full dataset.
Scales. Starting the y axis at zero, or not, can make a change look dramatic or trivial (see Chart scales).
Titles and annotations. A title which states a conclusion (‘Unemployment is falling’) tells the viewer what to see. An arrow drawn on a line chart tells them where to look (see Titles and labels and Annotations).

In 2012, the New York Times showed how the same monthly US jobs report could be presented in two ways: one framed as a Democrat might see it (unemployment falling steadily) and the other as a Republican might see it (unemployment still stubbornly high). The data was identical. Only the framing changed - the period shown, the annotations, and the headline.
None of this means you should avoid titles, annotations, or a clear message. A good chart should tell a story. But you should make those choices deliberately, be honest about them, and make sure the story is one the data actually supports.






Rhetoric you might not notice



Even design elements which don’t seem to say anything are persuasive. A source line (‘Source: World Bank’) lends a chart authority - sometimes called provenance rhetoric. A clean, minimal design signals that the chart is scientific and trustworthy, whether it is or not. Neither of these is bad in itself, but it’s worth noticing when a chart is borrowing authority it hasn’t earned.

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Objectivity, perspective and emotion
If every chart involves choices, can a chart ever be objective? Feminist scholars have offered some useful ways of thinking about this, which are summarised by Catherine D’Ignazio and Lauren Klein in their book Data Feminism.

The ‘god trick’. Donna Haraway described the kind of knowledge which claims to see everything from nowhere in particular - a view from above, by nobody - as a ‘god trick’. A chart which presents itself as a neutral view of the world is a good example. In fact, all knowledge is situated: it is made by particular people, in particular circumstances.
Positionality. Linda Alcoff and others use the term positionality to describe how each of us comes to knowledge from a particular position, shaped by things like gender, ethnicity, class, ability, education, and nationality. This affects both how a visualisation is made, and how it is read - including by you.
Strong objectivity. This doesn’t mean that anything goes. The philosopher Sandra Harding argued that being open about your perspective, and actively including perspectives which are usually left out, actually makes research more objective, not less. She called this ‘strong objectivity’.

This also raises the question of emotion. Data visualisation is often seen as the opposite of emotion: reason, numbers, and clean lines. But there’s no reason a chart can’t be both accurate and moving. Periscopic’s U.S. Gun Deaths (2013) shows each person killed by a gun in the US in one year as a single arc: the arc starts at their age when they died, and fades out at the age they might have lived to. The total at the top is not just the number of people killed, but the number of ‘stolen years’. The data is the same as you’d find in a table of statistics, but the design asks the viewer to see each death as a life.
For your own work, the practical lesson is: be transparent about your choices and your perspective. In your reports, say where your data came from, what you did to it, and what it can’t tell you.

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
section: When the data goes wrong: missing values
text:
When the data goes wrong: missing values
Some of the most important ethical decisions in data analysis look like small technical ones. One of the most common is what to do with missing data.
In 2019, a team of researchers published a high-profile paper in Nature using a large historical database of past societies. It argued that complex societies developed before ‘moralising gods’ (gods who punish bad behaviour), rather than the other way around. Other researchers soon found a problem: in many cases where the database had no information about whether a society had moralising gods, the analysis had treated this as meaning the society didn’t have them. In other words, missing data (NA) had been treated as a zero. The paper was retracted in 2021.
This is a mistake which is very easy to make in R, and it’s worth seeing how much difference it makes. The Titanic dataset is missing the age of 263 of its 1,309 passengers. Here’s the average age of passengers in each class, leaving the missing ages out (as you learned in the summarise chapter, using na.rm = TRUE):

Now let’s make the mistake on purpose. The code below uses mutate() and if_else() to replace every missing age with a zero, and then calculates the averages again:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The average age of third-class passengers has dropped by more than seven years - but first and second class have changed much less. Why? Let’s count how many passengers in each class have a missing age:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Almost a third of third-class passengers have no recorded age, compared to around one in twenty in second class. The data is not missing at random: the people the records know least about are the poorest passengers. Treating their missing ages as zero doesn’t just make the numbers wrong - it makes them wrong in a way which falls on one group in particular.
A chart makes this kind of mistake easy to spot, if you look. Here’s a histogram of ages, with the missing values replaced by zero:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
That spike at zero isn’t hundreds of babies - it’s hundreds of people whose ages nobody wrote down.






Missing data in your own work




Before you do anything else with a dataset, check where the NA values are, for example with summarise() and sum(is.na(column)).
Never replace NA with zero unless you’re sure that ‘no data’ really does mean ‘none’.
Ask whose data is missing. Missing data often tells you something about who collected the data and who they thought was important.
Say in your report how much data was missing, and what you did about it.

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Visualising people and sensitive topics
Many humanities datasets are about people, and some are about suffering: war, migration, slavery, disease. Design choices which are fine for a chart of book sales can be inappropriate here.

Think about what your shapes suggest. Arrows on a migration map are a common choice, but large, bold arrows also look like the arrows on maps of military invasions - and have been used in exactly that way in propaganda maps. Maps of refugees fleeing Ukraine in 2022 published by The Economist, for example, avoided large arrows and used circles sized by the number of people arriving in each country. Same data, very different message.
Remember that each data point is a person. A count of deaths is not like a count of books. Avoid sensationalist titles, jokey colours, or decorative design.
Consider showing individuals. Like the gun deaths example above, showing people as individual marks rather than one total can help viewers remember that the data is about lives.
Protect privacy. Be careful about publishing data, or maps, which could identify living individuals.
crumbs: Week 5 · Tue 24 Nov: Ethics, FAIR Data & Accessibility

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Data that challenges power
Data visualisation has often been used to reinforce injustice. In the 1930s, the US government’s ‘redlining’ maps graded neighbourhoods by their supposed mortgage risk, largely on the basis of the race of the people who lived there - and those grades shaped who could get a loan for decades (you can explore these maps with the Mapping Inequality project, listed on the data page).
But it has also been used to challenge it.

For the 1900 Paris Exposition, W.E.B. Du Bois and his students at Atlanta University made a series of strikingly modern hand-drawn charts showing the progress of Black Americans since the end of slavery - a direct challenge to the racist ideas of the time.
In 1971, the Detroit Geographic Expedition and Institute, a collaboration between a Black youth activist, Gwendolyn Warren, and geographers, made a map called Where Commuters Run Over Black Children on the Pointes-Downtown Track. No official data showed the problem, so the community collected its own. The map made visible something which the people in charge had not wanted to see.
In 2016, journalists at ProPublica investigated a computer system used by US courts to predict whether a defendant would reoffend. They collected their own dataset on thousands of real defendants, and found the predictions were only somewhat more accurate than a coin flip - and that Black defendants were much more likely to be wrongly labelled as high risk.

In each case, the people making the visualisation had to ask the questions from the start of this chapter: who collected the data, who is missing, and who benefits?

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
section: A checklist for your own visualisations
text:
A checklist for your own visualisations
The visualisation researcher Michael Correll has suggested some ethical goals for people who make visualisations. Adapted for this course, they make a useful checklist for your reports:

Make the invisible visible. Is there something important in your data (or missing from it) which your chart hides?
Show uncertainty. Be honest about what the data can’t tell you, and how reliable it is.
Remember the people in the data. Can your design help viewers remember that the data is about people?
Protect privacy. Could your chart, or the data you publish with it, identify anyone?
Question power. Whose perspective does the data represent? Who collected it, and why?

And here are some questions to ask of any visualisation, whether it’s yours or someone else’s:

Does it have a political or persuasive purpose? Is that purpose open, or hidden?
How was the data collected, and is this explained?
What role does emotion play? How does the chart present itself - as neutral and objective, or as a particular point of view?
Who is the chart about, and who is it for? Could it marginalise, or promote, particular groups?
What do you imagine is the position of the person who made it? What about your own position - how does it affect the way you read the chart?

title: 43  Ethics and data visualisation
text:
Check your understanding
1. A student is analysing a dataset of letters in an archive. The sender_gender column is NA for 40% of letters. To make a bar chart of letters by gender, they replace every NA with "male", because ‘most letter-writers in this period were men’. What’s the problem, and what would be a better approach?






Answer





They’ve turned an assumption into data. The chart will now show many more letters by men than the archive can actually support - and it will hide the fact that 40% of the senders are unknown, which is itself an important finding. A better approach would be to keep the unknown senders as their own category (e.g. ‘Unknown’) in the chart, or to leave them out and say clearly in the text how many letters were excluded. They might also ask why so many senders are unknown: are letters by women more likely to be unattributed?



2. A chart of the transatlantic slave trade uses bright red arrows of different thicknesses, and the title ‘The Great Migration Machine’. Give two ethical problems with this design.






Answer





Some possible answers:

The title is flippant and sensationalist, and ‘migration’ hides the fact that this was forced: it treats a history of enormous suffering as a curiosity.
Bold arrows suggest movement as a kind of force or flow, and turn people into an abstract stream. A more respectful design might show numbers of people more soberly, or show individual voyages or people.
Bright red is likely to come across as alarming or decorative rather than respectful (and may also be a problem for colour-blind viewers).
The chart should also say where the data comes from, and that the records were made by the people who carried out the trade.

title: 44  Reproducibility and FAIR data
text:
Reproducibility
An important principle in working with code and data is reproducibility. Reproducibility is a key part of scientific analysis: the idea that we should do work with the aim that anyone, given the same code, data, and methods, should be able to reproduce our work. This allows others to verify what we have done - that we haven’t accidentally (or maliciously) come to false conclusions.
To do this, we should generally publicly share the code and data in exactly the same formats, so others can recreate the exact same conditions.
crumbs: Week 5 · Tue 24 Nov: Ethics, FAIR Data & Accessibility

title: 44  Reproducibility and FAIR data
text:
Reproducibility with R
Luckily, our workflow makes this quite easy. R Markdown files will only ‘knit’ if they have access to the data and when the code works from beginning to end. To make the project reproducible, you can simply ensure that all data used is included along with the code. In a ‘live’ project, you would make this publicly available (checking copyright restrictions), on a code repository, usually Github or Zenodo.
For your final project, think about packaging everything up so that it is fully reproducible - so that I or anyone else could open the folder and run the code from start to finish and end up with an exact copy of your visualisation. Include your datasets in the .zip file with the Markdown. If you created any additional datasets, for example to help with data cleaning, make sure you include these too. If possible, download your data from online sources rather than loading it directly from the web. Include basic comments on your code, particularly anything which you think is unclear or might need explaining.






Versioning



A further aspect of reproducibility is ‘versioning’. R versions and packages change and this can cause problems for others running your code later on. To fix this you can use something called version control. R has a package renv to help with this. It essentially creates a fixed snapshot of R and its packages as you used them at the time you wrote your code, which others can download and use to run your code too. Practicing this is outside the scope of this course, but good to be aware of.

title: 44  Reproducibility and FAIR data
text:
FAIR Data
When working with data, you will often hear about how to make it FAIR. FAIR is a set of principles developed to make data as reusable as possible. The principles are:

Findable. This means making it easy to find your data, usually by adding keywords and making sure it is openly available and described correctly.
Accessible. In this context, accessible means making data publicly available, where possible.
Interoperable. Data should use existing standards and formats, so others can easily use or interact with it.
Reusable. Research data should be reusable by others - if data follows the above principles, plus is well documented, this will be the case.

How does this affect your own work? Primarily, you will be working on existing datasets when making visualisations on this course, but in many cases (on your own research project, for example), you might be responsible for creating datasets.
However, it’s worth bearing in mind the FAIR principles because they can be relevant in how you make your own work reusable. In most cases, you are the ‘end user’ of FAIR data, rather than creating it yourself. However you can ensure that the work you do also results in FAIR data, for example by describing and documenting your own work, and how you analysed or cleaned data.

Some general considerations for themes:

Make the font as large as is suitable for the image
Use a sans serif font
Use a black or dark grey text for annotations and labels of lines or segments
Use a lighter grey for axes labels so the important information stands out – see this colours guidance for more information

title: 45  Data Visualisation and Accessibility Considerations
text:
Alt-text
A final consideration, particularly when making charts which are to be viewed online, is to take into account readers who use screen-reading software. We should aim to provide alt-text for images, which will be read out loud by screen readers. In doing so, you should aim to summarise the visual elements and key points of the chart.

Alt Text defined from Webaim:

It is read by screen readers in place of images allowing the content and function of the image to be accessible to those with visual or certain cognitive disabilities.
It is displayed in place of the image in browsers if the image file is not loaded or when the user has chosen not to view images.
It provides a semantic meaning and description to images which can be read by search engines or be used to later determine the content of the image from page context alone.

The following is a good template to use for writing alt-text:


Chart type
It’s helpful for people with partial sight to know what chart type it is and gives context for understanding the rest of the visual.
Example: Line graph


Type of data
What data is included in the chart? The x and y axis labels may help you figure this out.
Example: number of bananas sold per day in the last year


Reason for including the chart
Think about why you’re including this visual. What does it show that’s meaningful. There should be a point to every visual and you should tell people what to look for.
Example: the winter months have more banana sales


Link to data or source
Don’t include this in your alt text, but it should be included somewhere in the surrounding text. People should be able to click on a link to view the source data or dig further into the visual. This provides transparency about your source and lets people explore the data.
Example: Data from the USDA



Adding alt-text in R Markdown.
You can add alt-text to static images or to generated plots made in code cells.
To add alt-text to R Markdown files, switch to the Source editor in Posit Cloud/RStudio.

Code cell options
We can add what are known as ‘cell options’, which allow us to edit how the result of a code cell is displayed in the knitted markdown file. In R Markdown, enter your code cell options between the first set of curly brackets, after the r. Leave a space, then each option, an equal sign, and the required value. Leave a comma in between each option.
You can use this to change the figure width and height in the output (fig.width and fig.height), whether or not the code is displayed in the finished file (echo=false), and many more.

title: 48  Maps as data visualisation
text:
Why make a map?
Maps are useful because some information has inherently spatial aspects - where the data is from is as important as what. We might want to understand geographic patterns of a phenomenon, for instance how language is used in different regions, or where cultural institutions are concentrated.
A map can also be a useful cognitive shortcut. Because we all have models of maps in our heads already (think about how you know roughly where the provinces of the Netherlands or the major cities of Europe are), we can often grasp a lot of information very quickly. If you know the rough positions of the provinces of the Netherlands, you will probably understand some data about them more quickly as a map than as a table.
Data maps also help us see patterns which are specifically geographic: that something is more common on coasts, in cities, or in particular regions, or that there are differences between the centre and the periphery.
But a map is not always the best choice. If the question you’re asking isn’t really about geography, a simple bar chart is often clearer. Ask yourself: does location actually matter here?

title: 48  Maps as data visualisation
text:
How computers store maps
There are two common ways of representing the real world as data: raster and vector maps. On this course we’ll work only with vector maps, but it’s useful to know the difference.

Raster maps
A raster map represents the world as a grid of pixels, like a digital photograph. Each pixel is coloured, and the colour means something. A scan of a historical map is a raster map; so is an elevation map, in which each pixel is coloured by the height of the land at that point:



Vector maps
A vector map instead represents geographic things as points, lines, and polygons (shapes), each stored as a set of coordinates. A city might be a point, a river a line, and a country a polygon. Unlike a raster map, a vector map knows that a certain shape is ‘the Netherlands’, so we can attach data to it - its population, its number of World Heritage sites, and so on. This is what makes vector data so useful for data visualisation.



A vector map containing rivers, cities, and country borders

title: 48  Maps as data visualisation
section: Maps map data to aesthetics, too
text:
Maps map data to aesthetics, too
Just as with every other chart on this course, making a data map means mapping data to aesthetics. The difference is that position is now a real place on the earth, rather than an x and y axis. On top of position, data maps mostly use colour, size, and shape. There are two main kinds:

Points maps
A points map draws a point at a specific location, such as a town, a building, or an address. This first example simply uses position: each Covid death in the US has been drawn as a single tiny point, and through millions of these points we can see where the death toll was highest.







Note



This map also shows one weakness of points maps: often, a map like this simply shows where people live, rather than revealing anything new. Always ask whether your map is just a population map in disguise!



https://xkcd.com/1138/




We can also map further aesthetics to the points. In this example from the New York Times, each point is a weather station where a temperature record was broken. The colour shows whether it was a heat (red) or cold (blue) record, and the size shows by how much the previous record was broken:



Choropleth maps
The other main kind of data map colours in regions - countries, provinces, municipalities - according to some data. This is called a choropleth map. Choropleths are useful when your data isn’t about a single point, but about an area. Election maps are a classic example, because votes are counted by region. In this map of the 2011 Dutch provincial elections, each municipality is coloured by the party which won the most votes there:



The trouble with choropleths
Choropleths are very common, but they can easily mislead. In the election map above, about half of the map is blue. You might think that the VVD received around half of the votes. In fact, they won about one-fifth.
This is because the map gives every square kilometre the same visual weight, but votes are cast by people, not land. The VVD did well in rural areas, which are large but sparsely populated. A good rule in data visualisation is that the same amount of ‘ink’ should represent the same amount of data - and a choropleth often breaks this rule.
There are two common ways to deal with this:

Normalise the data. Instead of mapping raw counts (the number of World Heritage sites in a country, say), map a rate: sites per million people, or per square kilometre. Otherwise, big countries will tend to look ‘more’ of everything. Choosing what to divide by is itself an important decision - we’ll come back to this next class.
Distort the map. A cartogram resizes regions according to the data. This example resizes the countries of the EU according to how much they contributed to, or received from, the EU budget per person between 2007 and 2013:




Every map is a choice
Maps feel objective - they look like a picture of the world as it is. But every map involves choices: which places to include, which borders to draw (and from which year), which projection to use, which data to show, and what to leave out. Borders themselves are often contested. It’s always worth asking who made a map, for what purpose, and whose view of the world it represents.

text:
Getting a map
The function ne_countries() downloads a map of all the world’s countries. It needs two arguments:
Save the result as an object, so we can use it later:

title: 49  Your first map
text:
scale = sets how detailed the borders are: 'small' or 'medium'. (There’s also 'large', but it needs an extra package and is far more detail than we need.)
returnclass = 'sf' tells it to give us the map in the format the sf package uses, called simple features. We’ll always use this.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Tip



You can also download individual countries, e.g. ne_countries(country = c('Netherlands', 'Belgium'), scale = 'medium', returnclass = 'sf'), or a map of coastlines without any borders, with ne_coastline(scale = 'medium', returnclass = 'sf').

title: 49  Your first map
section: What is a simple features object?
text:
What is a simple features object?
Let’s look at the map. It’s a big object, so we’ll just select() a few of its columns:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
It looks very much like the dataframes we’ve been working with all along. Each row is one country, and there are columns with information about it - its name, continent, population (pop_est), and much more. In geographic terms, each row is called a feature.
The difference is the extra column at the end: geometry. This contains the shape of each country, as a long list of coordinates which, joined together, draw its outline. Notice that we didn’t ask for the geometry column in select(), but it’s still there: in an sf object, the geometry ‘sticks’ to each row, whatever you do to it.
Geometries can be points, lines, or polygons (shapes):



Examples of different geographic features. Countries are usually polygons, or multipolygons if they’re made up of several shapes, such as a mainland and islands.


Above the table, you’ll also see a line starting Geodetic CRS. This is the map’s coordinate reference system, which tells R how the coordinates relate to real places on the earth. We’ll come back to this in the chapter on projections.

title: 49  Your first map
text:
Drawing a map with geom_sf()
To draw a map, we use ggplot2 exactly as before, with a new geom: geom_sf(). Unlike geom_point() or geom_col(), we don’t need to tell it what goes on the x and y axes - it reads the positions from the geometry column.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
That’s it - a map of the world!

sf objects work with dplyr
Because an sf object behaves like a dataframe, we can use all the dplyr functions we’ve learned on it. For example, Antarctica takes up a lot of space at the bottom of the map. Let’s remove it with filter(), and save the result:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Try it yourself: make a map of only the countries of Africa.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 49  Your first map
text:
Colouring the map by data
Now we can turn this into a data visualisation. As with any other chart, we map a column to an aesthetic inside aes(). For polygons, the most useful aesthetic is fill. Let’s fill each country by its continent:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Because continent is a categorical variable, ggplot uses a categorical colour scale. If we use a numeric column, such as population, we get a continuous scale instead:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Inside or outside aes()?



The same rule applies as for every other chart. Put an aesthetic inside aes() when it should depend on the data. Put it outside aes() when you want to set it to one fixed value - for example, to make all the borders white and thin:
geom_sf(data = worldmap, aes(fill = pop_est), colour = 'white', linewidth = 0.1)
For polygons, fill is the colour of the inside of the shape, and colour is the colour of its border.

title: 49  Your first map
section: Making it look like a map
text:
Making it look like a map
The grey background, grid lines, and latitude/longitude labels are useful for a chart, but they usually aren’t needed on a map. The quickest way to remove them is theme_void(). Then we can use everything we’ve learned about scales and labels to finish the map:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Warning



This map makes a good example, but not a very interesting one: big countries with lots of people stand out, as you’d expect. Next class we’ll see how to normalise data, so that countries of different sizes can be compared fairly.


Try it yourself: the map has a column called income_grp, which puts each country into one of five income groups. Make a map filled by income group, with thin grey borders, a title, a better legend title, and theme_void().

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 49  Your first map
text:
Zooming in
Often, we want to map only part of the world. There are two ways of doing this, and they do different things.

Filtering
The first is to filter() the data, as we did with Antarctica. Let’s try making a map of Europe:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
That’s not what we wanted! The problem is that some European countries have territories elsewhere in the world. France, for example, includes French Guiana in South America, so the map has to stretch to fit it in. Russia also stretches all the way to the Pacific.


Zooming with coord_sf()
The second way is to keep all the data, but tell ggplot which area to show, using coord_sf(). This is the coordinates layer, which we’ve skipped over until now. Its xlim and ylim arguments set the range of longitude (east-west) and latitude (north-south) to show:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Often, the best approach is a combination: filter to the data you need, and zoom with coord_sf() to choose the area. Zooming in with coord_sf() also means neighbouring countries are drawn at the edges, which helps readers find their way:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This last map has two geom_sf() layers: first the whole world in grey, and then Europe on top, in blue. As with every ggplot, layers are drawn in order, so the layer you want on top must come last.






Finding the right limits



To find the longitude and latitude of an area, you can look it up on a map: for example, right-clicking on a place in Google Maps shows its coordinates (latitude first, then longitude). West of Greenwich and south of the equator are negative numbers.


Try it yourself: adjust the limits to zoom in on Scandinavia.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note



Zooming doesn’t change the data, only the view. If you colour countries by some data and then zoom in, the colour scale is still based on all the countries, including the ones you can’t see. If this matters, filter the data first.

Check your understanding
1. A student’s map has the countries coloured in, but no borders are visible. What would they add to geom_sf() to draw the borders in white?






Answer





colour = 'white', outside aes(): geom_sf(data = worldmap, aes(fill = continent), colour = 'white'). For polygons, colour controls the border, and fill the inside.



2. What’s the difference between these two maps?
worldmap |> filter(continent == 'Asia') |> ggplot() + geom_sf()

worldmap |> ggplot() + geom_sf() + coord_sf(xlim = c(25, 150), ylim = c(-10, 60))

The first only draws the countries whose continent is Asia (and the map stretches to fit all of them in). The second draws all the countries, but zooms in on the area from 25° to 150° east and 10° south to 60° north, so neighbouring countries (and parts of Europe and Africa) are visible at the edges.



3. In the code ggplot() + geom_sf(data = worldmap), why don’t we need to give an x and y aesthetic?

Because geom_sf() reads the positions from the special geometry column of the sf object, which contains the coordinates of each shape.

title: 50  Map projections
text:
What gets distorted?
A projection can preserve some properties of the earth’s surface, but never all of them at once:

title: 50  Map projections
text:
Area: the relative sizes of places.
Shape (or angles): the shapes of places, at least locally.
Distance: the distances between places.




The three families of map projection: the globe is projected onto a cylinder (a), a cone (b), or a flat plane (c), which is then unrolled.

title: 50  Map projections
text:
Changing the projection with coord_sf()
The maps we made in the last chapter used a very simple ‘projection’: longitude was used directly as the x axis, and latitude as the y axis. This is easy, but it stretches everything away from the equator.
To change the projection, we use the coordinates layer again: coord_sf(), with the argument crs =. crs stands for coordinate reference system (more on this below). Each projection has a code, which we pass to crs as a text string starting with +proj=.

Mercator
The Mercator projection is the one you probably know best, because it’s used by Google Maps and most online maps:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Mercator preserves shape: a small island has the right shape, and a constant compass direction is a straight line, which made it very useful for navigation at sea. But it hugely distorts area towards the poles. Greenland looks about the size of Africa, when Africa is actually around fourteen times larger. For a data map, this matters: countries far from the equator - in Europe and North America, for instance - look much bigger, and so more important, than they are.


Equal-area projections
An equal-area projection preserves the relative sizes of places, at the cost of distorting their shapes. For choropleth maps, where we colour in regions, this is usually what we want: otherwise, the area of colour a reader sees depends on the projection as well as on the data. The Equal Earth projection is a good modern choice:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Compare the sizes of Greenland and Africa with the Mercator map above.
Another common equal-area projection is Mollweide ('+proj=moll'):



The Mollweide equal-area projection.




Compromise projections
A compromise projection doesn’t preserve any one property exactly, but tries to keep all the distortions reasonably small, so the map ‘looks right’. These are good for general-purpose world maps. The Robinson projection is a well-known example:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Try it yourself: draw the world map, filled by continent, in the Mollweide projection ('+proj=moll'), and the Winkel Tripel projection ('+proj=wintri'), which is used by National Geographic. Which do you prefer?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 50  Map projections
text:
Projections for smaller areas
Projections matter most for world maps, but they matter for smaller areas too. For maps of Europe, Eurostat (the EU’s statistical office) uses an equal-area projection with the code 3035. Codes like this are called EPSG codes, and you give them to crs as a number rather than text.
There’s one catch: in a projected map, the coordinates are no longer longitude and latitude, but distances in metres. So if we zoom in with xlim and ylim, we need to tell coord_sf() that our limits are still in longitude and latitude, by setting default_crs to 4326 (the code for ordinary longitude and latitude):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Compare this to the map of Europe in the last chapter: Scandinavia is no longer stretched, and the map curves the way the earth does.






Note



The lines of longitude and latitude are now curved, so a ‘box’ of longitude and latitude no longer fits the map neatly. ggplot uses the corners of your limits to decide what to show, which means the edges of the area can get cut off. If that happens, just make the limits a little wider.








Tip



For a map of the Netherlands, the official Dutch projection is EPSG code 28992 (‘Amersfoort / RD New’). Most countries have their own standard projection: search for ‘[country] EPSG’ to find it.

title: 50  Map projections
text:
Coordinate reference systems
You’ll often see the term coordinate reference system (CRS) in connection with maps. A CRS is the full set of rules which links the numbers in the geometry column to real places on the earth. There are two types:

A geographic CRS uses longitude and latitude, in degrees. The most common is called WGS 84, with the EPSG code 4326. This is what GPS uses, and it’s the CRS of the Natural Earth maps.




A geographic CRS: positions are given as degrees of longitude and latitude.



A projected CRS uses a flat, projected map, with positions measured in metres from some starting point. EPSG 3035 and 28992 are both projected CRSs.




A projected CRS: the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system divides the world into zones, each with its own flat grid.


You can check the CRS of any sf object with st_crs():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Why does this matter?
Most of the time, ggplot takes care of the CRS for you. When you add several geom_sf() layers to one map, ggplot converts them all to the same CRS: the one set in coord_sf(), or, if you haven’t set one, the CRS of the first layer.
Where it does matter is when you make your own sf object, for example from a set of coordinates. Then you’ll need to tell R which CRS your coordinates use. We’ll do this in the chapter on points maps.






Note



You might also come across the sf function st_transform(), which permanently converts an sf object to a different CRS, e.g. worldmap |> st_transform(crs = '+proj=eqearth'). For drawing maps with ggplot, coord_sf(crs = ...) does the same job.

title: 50  Map projections
text:
Check your understanding
1. You’re making a choropleth map of the world, showing the number of museums per person in each country. Which kind of projection should you choose, and why?






Answer





An equal-area projection, such as Equal Earth or Mollweide. In a choropleth, readers judge the data partly by how much area is coloured. A projection which enlarges some regions, like Mercator (which makes countries near the poles look much bigger), would give those countries more visual weight than the data justifies.



2. Why does Greenland look as big as Africa on many online maps?






Answer





Most online maps use the Mercator projection, which preserves shapes but increasingly exaggerates areas towards the poles.

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
text:
The six steps of a choropleth map
Making a choropleth map from your own data always involves the same steps. We’ll go through each one in turn:
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
text:
Get to know your data, and work out its geographic unit (countries? provinces? municipalities?).
Find a map with features (shapes) for that same geographic unit.
Find a common field: a column in your data and a column in the map which identify the places in the same way.
Summarise your data, so there’s one row for each place on the map.
Join the summarised data to the map, with left_join().
Draw the map, and think carefully about what you’re showing.
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
section: Step 1: Get to know your data
text:
Step 1: Get to know your data
The World Heritage List is published by UNESCO as open data. I’ve made a slightly simplified version for this course. Let’s load the packages we need and read it in:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Why na = ""?



By default, read_csv() treats any cell containing the text NA as a missing value. Usually that’s helpful - but in this dataset, NA is also the country code for Namibia! Setting na = "" tells R that only empty cells are missing. This is a good example of why you should always check your data after reading it in.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each row is one World Heritage site, with its name, its category (Cultural, Natural or Mixed), the year it was added to the list (date_inscribed), whether it’s on the list of sites ‘in danger’, and the country or countries it’s in, both as names (states) and as two-letter codes (iso_codes). There are also coordinates, which we’ll use for a points map in the next class.
Before mapping anything, it’s always worth exploring the data with the tools we already know. For example, UNESCO divides the world into five regions:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Almost half of all World Heritage sites are in the region ‘Europe and North America’. Keep this in mind as we go.

What’s the geographic unit?
The geographic unit of this data is the country - or, in UNESCO’s terms, the ‘State Party’ which nominated the site. So we need a map of the world’s countries.
But there’s a complication. Some sites cross borders, and are listed under more than one country:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The forest of Białowieża, for example, is in both Poland (PL) and Belarus (BY). We’ll deal with this in step 4.
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
text:
Step 2: Find a map
For countries, the Natural Earth world map we used last class is ideal:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
For other geographic units - provinces, municipalities, historical borders - you’ll need to find and load a different map. That’s covered in the next chapter.
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
text:
Step 3: Find a common field
To join two datasets, we need a column in each which identifies the same thing in the same way. We could try country names, but names are risky. UNESCO calls the UK ‘United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland’, while Natural Earth calls it ‘United Kingdom’, so they wouldn’t match. Names can also be spelled differently, or written in different languages.
It’s much better to use a standard code, where one is available. For countries, the most common are the ISO codes: two letters (NL) or three letters (NLD). Our data has two-letter codes in the iso_codes column. The world map has a lot of columns with codes in them, but the one we want is called iso_a2_eh:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note



Notice that the column iso_a2 gives France and Norway the code -99, meaning ‘missing’. That’s for complicated technical reasons to do with their overseas territories. The column iso_a2_eh fixes this, which is why we use it instead. Little traps like this are very common when joining data, so always check your join (see step 5).
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
text:
Step 4: Summarise your data
The map has one row per country, so our data needs one row per country too. Right now, it has one row per site. We need to count the sites in each country.
First, though, we need to deal with the cross-border sites. The function separate_rows() (from tidyr) splits a column containing several values into separate rows. Here, it splits iso_codes at each comma:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now Białowieża Forest has two rows: one for Poland, and one for Belarus. This means a cross-border site will count once for each country it’s in, which seems fair.
Now we can count the number of sites for each country code, using count(). The argument name = sets the name of the new column:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
section: Step 5: Join the data to the map
text:
Step 5: Join the data to the map
Now we can join the two together, with left_join(). The map must be on the left, so that the result is still a map (an sf object), and so that every country is kept, even if it has no sites. Because the common columns have different names, we tell left_join() which column in the map matches which column in our data with by = c('map column' = 'data column'):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Check the join
Always check that a join has done what you expected. A good start is to look for rows that didn’t match, which will have NA in the new column:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Most of these are countries which really have no World Heritage sites. Some are places which aren’t independent countries, like Jersey or Aruba, and some, like Taiwan, aren’t members of UNESCO at all. Greenland is here too: UNESCO lists its sites under Denmark. We’ll treat them all as having zero sites - but note that, for Taiwan, ‘zero’ means ‘can’t have any’, not ‘has none’.
Next, check whether any places on the map share the same code. If they do, they’ll both be given the same number of sites. We can find them by grouping by the code, and keeping only the groups with more than one row:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Somaliland, Northern Cyprus and the Siachen Glacier share the ‘missing’ code -99, which doesn’t matter, as none of them has any sites. But two Australian territories - the Indian Ocean Territories and the uninhabited Ashmore and Cartier Islands - have each been given Australia’s 21 sites! Natural Earth draws some territories separately from their country, but gives them the country’s code. These territories have the type ‘Dependency’. Let’s remove them, and replace the remaining NA values with zero using replace_na():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
crumbs: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map

title: 52  Choropleth maps: joining your data to a map
text:
Step 6: Draw the map
Now we can draw the map, filling each country by its number of sites. Following the chapter on projections, we’ll use an equal-area projection:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Binning the colour scale
With a continuous colour scale, it’s hard for readers to tell exactly which value a colour stands for. On maps, it’s often clearer to bin the scale into a few groups, each with its own colour. The _b version of the viridis scale does this. We can set where the bins start and end with breaks =:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
direction = -1 reverses the colours, so that the countries with the most sites are the darkest, which most readers expect.


Normalising the data
This map shows that Italy, China, France, Germany and Spain have the most sites. But as we saw in the first mapping chapter, maps of raw counts are often dominated by big countries. Bigger countries have more room for more sites.
To compare countries of different sizes, we can normalise the data: divide it by something that accounts for size. Let’s try the number of sites per million people:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The Vatican has two World Heritage sites and only around 800 inhabitants, so it has well over 2,000 sites per million people. Tiny countries like this would dominate any scale. One option is to leave them out, and say so on the map. Here, we’ll only include countries with at least one million people, and draw the others in grey (by setting their value to NA, and choosing a colour for NA with na.value =):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The two maps tell quite different stories. In the first, China and India stand out. In the second, Europe stands out even more strongly, as do countries with small populations, such as Mongolia, while China and India fall to the lowest group.


What are we actually measuring?
Which map is ‘right’? Neither, on its own. Dividing by population answers a different question to dividing by area, and neither tells us how much heritage a country has. That’s because the list doesn’t measure heritage. It records which places have been nominated by governments and accepted by a UNESCO committee.
Making a nomination takes money, expertise, and political will. For decades, the criteria favoured the kinds of heritage valued in Europe, such as cathedrals, palaces, and historic town centres, over, for example, living traditions or sacred landscapes. UNESCO itself recognised this imbalance in 1994, when it launched a ‘Global Strategy’ to make the list more representative.
It’s always worth asking: who made this data, for what purpose, and whose idea of value does it represent? A good map - and a good report - should make this clear to the reader, for example in the title, the caption, or the text around it.

Check your understanding
1. Why should the map be on the left side of left_join()?






Answer





left_join() keeps every row of the left-hand dataset, so with the map on the left, every country stays on the map, even those with no data. The result also keeps the class of the left-hand object, so it’s still an sf object which geom_sf() can draw. With the data on the left, countries with no data would disappear, and the result would be an ordinary dataframe.



2. After a join, a country that you know has data shows up in grey (NA). Give two possible reasons.






Answer





The codes or names don’t match: for example, a spelling difference (‘Czechia’ vs ‘Czech Republic’), a different kind of code (two-letter vs three-letter ISO codes), or a missing-value code such as -99 in the map. Or the data itself has a problem, such as a code read in as NA (like Namibia’s NA code), or the country being recorded under a different name or historical state.



3. A student maps the total number of museums in each country of Europe, and concludes that Germany and France are the most ‘museum-rich’ countries. What’s the problem, and how could they fix it?






Answer





Raw counts mostly reflect the size of the countries: big countries with many people will usually have more museums. To compare countries fairly, they should normalise the data, e.g. museums per 100,000 people. They should also be clear about what the data actually measures - for instance, how ‘museum’ was defined, and by whom.

title: 53  Finding and reading map files
text:
Where to find map files
Map files with official boundaries are usually published by government agencies, often for free. Some good places to look:
crumbs: 53  Finding and reading map files

title: 53  Finding and reading map files
text:
The Netherlands: PDOK and CBS publish boundaries of provinces, municipalities, neighbourhoods and more. The cartomap project makes simplified versions of the CBS boundaries for every year, which are ideal for data maps (the maps in this chapter come from there).
Europe: Eurostat publishes the boundaries of the EU’s statistical regions, called NUTS regions, at three levels: NUTS 1 (large regions) to NUTS 3 (small regions). A lot of EU data is published by NUTS region, so these are very useful.
The whole world: geoBoundaries has open boundaries of regions and provinces for almost every country.







Historical maps



Boundaries change over time, and a map of modern borders often isn’t suitable for historical data. There are also many projects which publish historical boundaries, such as the Historical GIS of the Low Countries and A Vision of Britain Through Time.
crumbs: 53  Finding and reading map files

title: 53  Finding and reading map files
text:
Map file formats
You’ll come across map files in several formats. The three most common are:

GeoJSON (.geojson or .json): a single text file. Very common for maps published online.
Shapefile (.shp): an older but still very common format. A shapefile is actually a set of files with the same name and different endings, such as .shp (the shapes), .dbf (the data about each shape), and .prj (the projection). You read in the .shp file, but all the other files must be in the same folder. Shapefiles are usually downloaded as a .zip file: unzip it (or upload the zip to Posit Cloud, which unzips it), and keep the files together.
GeoPackage (.gpkg): a newer format, which can contain several maps (called layers) in a single file.

The good news is that the sf package reads all of them with the same function: st_read().

title: 53  Finding and reading map files
section: Reading a map file with st_read()
text:
Reading a map file with st_read()
Let’s load the packages, and download the map of the Dutch provinces, which is a GeoJSON file:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now read it in with st_read(), giving it the name of the file:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
st_read() prints a short summary: there are 12 features (the provinces), they’re multipolygons, and the CRS is WGS 84, i.e. ordinary longitude and latitude. Let’s look at the data, and draw it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
As well as the names of the provinces (statnaam), there’s a column called statcode, with a code for each province: PV20 for Groningen, PV28 for Zuid-Holland, and so on. These are the codes CBS uses in its statistics, which will be very useful for joining.






Reading shapefiles and GeoPackages



Shapefiles are read in exactly the same way, giving the path to the .shp file:
regions <- st_read("NUTS_RG_60M_2024_4326/NUTS_RG_60M_2024_4326.shp")
A GeoPackage may contain several layers. Use st_layers() to list them, and then pick one with layer =:
st_layers("wijkenbuurten_2024.gpkg")
municipalities <- st_read("wijkenbuurten_2024.gpkg", layer = "gemeenten")

text:
Joining data to the provinces
The number of national monuments in each province and municipality is published by CBS, the Dutch statistics office. I’ve downloaded the figures for 2024:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The data is in a ‘long’ format: for each region, there’s one row for each type of monument (archaeology, religious buildings, farms and mills, and so on), plus a row for the total. The regions include both provinces (with codes starting PV) and municipalities (GM).
Following the six steps, our geographic unit is the province, our map is provinces, and the common field is the CBS code. Next, we need one row per province, so let’s filter to the provinces and the total number of monuments:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The obvious way to join the two is by the names of the provinces. Let’s try it, with the map on the left:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Every value is NA - nothing has matched! Let’s compare the names in the two datasets:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
In the CBS data, every province name has ’ (PV)’ added at the end (for provincie), so ‘Groningen’ in the map doesn’t match ‘Groningen (PV)’ in the data. We could fix this by removing the extra text with str_remove(). But as we saw in the last chapter, it’s more reliable to join on a code, if one is available - and here, both datasets have the CBS code:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now the join works. Let’s draw the map:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Noord-Holland, which includes Amsterdam, has by far the most.

title: 53  Finding and reading map files
text:
Going further: municipalities
Provinces are large, and hide a lot of variation. Let’s do the same at the level of the municipality (gemeente), of which there were 342 in 2025:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A few municipalities, such as Amsterdam, have thousands of monuments, while most have a few hundred at most. With a continuous colour scale, almost every municipality would get the same colour. A binned scale, with bins that get wider as the numbers get bigger, shows the variation much better:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The big cities stand out, as you’d expect - but what do you notice about the north of the country? The first exercise below will help you find out what’s going on.






Match the year of your data and your map



Boundaries change. Dutch municipalities merge with each other almost every year, so the list of municipalities in 2025 is different to the list in 2020. Always use a map of the boundaries from the same year as your data. CBS makes this easier by saying which year’s boundaries it used: this data uses the 2025 boundaries (‘indeling 2025’), so we use the 2025 map. If your data and map come from different years, some places won’t match.

1. A student downloads a shapefile as a zip, unzips it, and uploads only the .shp file to Posit Cloud. When they run st_read(), they get an error. Why?






Answer





A shapefile is a set of files (.shp, .dbf, .prj, and others), and st_read() needs all of them, in the same folder. They need to upload all the files, not just the .shp.



2. A student joins a dataset of library loans by municipality in 2015 to a map of the municipalities in 2025. Some municipalities don’t match. What’s the most likely reason?






Answer





Municipal boundaries have changed between 2015 and 2025: many municipalities have merged, so some 2015 municipalities no longer exist, and some 2025 municipalities didn’t exist yet. They should use a map of the 2015 boundaries.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Latitude and longitude
To draw a point, we need its coordinates: two numbers which give its position on the earth.
Coordinates can be written in decimal form (Leiden is at latitude 52.16, longitude 4.49) or in degrees, minutes and seconds (52° 9' 36" N, 4° 29' 49" E). In decimal form, places south of the equator and west of Greenwich have negative numbers: Buenos Aires is at -34.60, -58.38. We’ll always use decimal coordinates.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Latitude measures the north-south position, from +90° at the North Pole to -90° at the South Pole, with the equator at 0°.
Longitude measures the east-west position, from -180° to +180°. 0° is a line running through Greenwich, in London, known as the prime meridian.




Latitude (left) and longitude (right). Source: Wikipedia









Note



Latitude is like the y axis of a chart, and longitude like the x axis. But people usually write coordinates with latitude first - so it’s easy to mix them up. If your points end up in the sea, or the map looks mirrored, check that you haven’t swapped them!

title: 54  Points maps
section: Turning coordinates into an sf object
text:
Turning coordinates into an sf object
Let’s load the packages and the data:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The latitude and longitude columns are just numbers in a regular dataframe. To draw them with geom_sf(), we need to turn the dataframe into an sf object, with a geometry column. The function st_as_sf() does this. It needs:

The dataframe.
coords =: the names of the columns with the coordinates, as a vector, with the longitude (x) first, then the latitude (y).
crs =: the coordinate reference system the coordinates use. Ordinary longitude and latitude, as used by GPS and most datasets, is EPSG code 4326 (see the chapter on projections).

A few sites are missing coordinates (mostly sites only added to the list in 2026), and st_as_sf() will give an error if there are missing values, so we filter them out first:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The latitude and longitude columns have gone, and there’s now a geometry column, where each feature is a POINT.






Note



Sites which cross borders only have a single point. The Wadden Sea, for instance, is shared by the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, but its point is in Germany. When you put data on a map, you’ll often have to simplify like this - and you should say so in your report.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Drawing points with geom_sf()
We draw points in exactly the same way as polygons, with geom_sf():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You can almost see the shape of the continents. But to read a points map, people need to know where the points are, so we usually need a basemap underneath: a map of countries or coastlines which gives the reader context.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Adding a basemap
A basemap is just another geom_sf() layer, drawn before the points so that it sits underneath them. Let’s use the Natural Earth world map, in a light grey with white borders, so that it doesn’t distract from the data:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Mapping data to points
With points, we can use the aesthetics colour, size, shape and alpha (transparency). Let’s colour the points by the category of the site. With over a thousand points, many will overlap, so we’ll also make them small, and partly transparent with alpha, so that we can see where they’re stacked on top of each other. We’ll also use an equal-area projection:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Notice that we only needed to set the projection once, in coord_sf(): ggplot projects every layer, so the points and the basemap still line up.






Tip



Colour is set outside aes() for the basemap (fill = 'grey90'), because it’s a fixed value, and inside aes() for the points (colour = category), because it depends on the data. Points use colour, not fill.


Try it yourself: make a map of only the Natural sites, with the size of each point mapped to the area of the site (area_hectares). Does this work well? Why, or why not?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Zooming in, and overlapping points
The world map makes it look like Europe is one big blob of points. Let’s zoom in, using coord_sf() with the European projection (EPSG 3035) we used in the projections chapter:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Even zoomed in, some areas, such as Italy, are crowded. Overplotting - points hiding other points - is the most common problem with points maps. Some ways to deal with it:

Make the points smaller, or more transparent (alpha).
Zoom in on a smaller area.
Split the map into several small maps with facets (see below).
Summarise the points by region, and make a choropleth instead. If what matters is how many sites there are in each country, the choropleth in the last class is the better map. A points map is better for showing exactly where things are.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Highlighting some points
Sometimes, we want to draw attention to a subset of the data. Here, let’s highlight the 58 sites which are on UNESCO’s list of World Heritage in danger: sites threatened by war, natural disasters, uncontrolled development, or other dangers. We draw all the sites in grey first, and then the sites in danger on top, in red:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The pattern is very different to the list as a whole: many of the sites in danger are in the Middle East and Africa, including areas affected by war.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Small multiples with facets
Has the geography of the list changed over time? We can use facet_wrap() to make a separate small map for each period, just as with any other ggplot chart. First, we make a new column with case_when(), putting each site into a period depending on the year it was added to the list:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
It’s hard to see a big change by eye. This is where it helps to combine a map with a simple summary of the data. Let’s count the share of sites from each period in the region ‘Europe and North America’:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
(st_drop_geometry() turns an sf object back into a regular dataframe, which makes summaries quicker and tidier.)
Europe and North America’s share of new sites peaked at 55% in the 1990s, and has since fallen to around 40% - still far more than its share of the world’s population. A map can show where, but it’s often the combination of a map, a chart, and a few numbers that tells the full story.

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Checklist: finishing a map
When you make a map for your report, go through this checklist:

Is a map the best way to show this data? Does location actually matter?
Is the data normalised, if it’s a choropleth? Or have you explained why not?
Have you chosen a suitable projection (equal-area for choropleths of large areas)?
Have you zoomed in on the area that matters, and filtered out data you don’t need?
Is the colour scale suitable for the data (categorical, sequential, binned?), and readable by colour-blind readers?
Does the basemap help the reader, without distracting from the data?
Have you removed unnecessary elements (e.g. with theme_void())?
Does it have a clear title, a legend title, and a caption with the source of the data and the map?
Have you explained the choices and simplifications you made, and their limitations?

title: 54  Points maps
text:
Check your understanding
1. A student makes an sf object with st_as_sf(df, coords = c('latitude', 'longitude'), crs = 4326). What will go wrong?






Answer





The coordinates are in the wrong order: coords needs the longitude (x) first, then the latitude (y). With them swapped, every point will be drawn in the wrong place (Leiden, at latitude 52 and longitude 4, would end up at longitude 52 and latitude 4 - in the Indian Ocean).



2. A points map shows the basemap, but no points, although the code gives no error. The code is below. What’s wrong?
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = whc_points, colour = 'red') +
  geom_sf(data = worldmap, fill = 'grey90')






Answer





The layers are in the wrong order. ggplot draws layers in the order they’re added, so the basemap is drawn on top of the points, hiding them. The basemap should come first.



3. You have a dataset of 5,000 historical letters, each with the town it was sent from. Would you make a points map or a choropleth? What problems might you run into?






Answer





A points map, because the data is about specific towns, not regions. But you’d need to find coordinates for each town (see the next chapter), and many letters will come from the same towns, so the points would be drawn on top of each other. It would be better to first count the letters from each town with group_by() and summarise(), and then map the counts to the size of the points.

title: 55  Finding coordinates
text:
Looking them up by hand
If you have a small number of well-known, modern places (say, a list of capital cities), the simplest method is to look them up. Each place on Wikipedia has its coordinates at the top right of the page: click on them to find the decimal version. Google Maps also shows the coordinates of any point if you right-click on it (latitude first, then longitude). Add them to two new columns in your spreadsheet, called latitude and longitude.
This is slow, but it’s accurate, and you can be sure you have the right place.

title: 55  Finding coordinates
text:
Gazetteers
If you have many places, or historical places, or places in several languages, you could use a gazetteer. A gazetteer is a geographical dictionary: a list of place names, with information about each one, including coordinates.

GeoNames is the best-known general gazetteer, with around 12 million place names.
Pleiades is a gazetteer of places in the ancient world.
The World Historical Gazetteer collects historical place names from many sources and periods.

Most gazetteers let you download their whole dataset. You can then match your place names to the gazetteer with a left_join(), exactly as we joined data to maps - the place name (or, better, an identifier) is the common field.
Be careful, though. Place names are messy, especially historical ones. The same place can have many names, in different languages and periods (Leiden, Lugdunum Batavorum, Leyde), and many different places share the same name (there are dozens of places called Springfield). If you match place names automatically, always check the results by hand, and plot them on a map to spot points in obviously wrong places.

title: 55  Finding coordinates
text:
Geocoding services
A geocoding service takes a list of place names or addresses, looks each one up in a large database, and returns the coordinates. This is the quickest way to geocode a large number of modern places or addresses. Because they use the full address, they can usually tell the difference between Dublin in Ireland and Dublin in Ohio, if you include the country.
Most are commercial services with a free allowance, such as Geoapify, where you can upload a spreadsheet of addresses and download it again with coordinates added. In R, the package tidygeocoder can geocode a column of addresses using several services, including the free OpenStreetMap service, Nominatim.
Geocoding services are built for modern addresses, and often give poor results for historical places. As with gazetteers, check the results.

title: 55  Finding coordinates
text:
Which method should I use?

Choosing a method






Your data
Best method




A few well-known, modern places
Look them up by hand


Many historical or ancient places
A specialist gazetteer (e.g. Pleiades, World Historical Gazetteer)


Many modern places or addresses
A geocoding service



Whatever method you use, record what you did in your report, so that others can reproduce it - and be honest about places you couldn’t find, or weren’t sure about. Every point on a map is a claim that something happened there.
