title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Importing a dataset and dataset standards
For these assignments, you’ll need to begin by importing your dataset as an object into the RStudio/Posit environment. How you do this depends a little on the standard of your dataset. As we’re working with tabular data on this course, your data should in most cases be in one of these formats:
You can read data originating from either your local machine, or directly from the internet in some cases.
Whatever dataset you use, a really important task is to read the documentation available, so you understand, as best as possible, how it was made and who was responsible for it. If you can’t find out where a dataset came from, don’t use it.

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Comma separated values (files ending in .csv). A very common tabular data format. Use read_csv() from the Tidyverse package readr (remember to load the package first) to read the file in to Posit.
Tab separated values (files ending in .tsv). Another common tabular format. Use read_tsv() from the Tidyverse package readr to read the file.
Excel files: Microsoft proprietary format, which can contain multiple sheets. Use read_excel() from the Tidyverse package readxl to read the file.
Google sheets. You can read Google sheets directly from the internet using the package googlesheets4.



If you’re loading from your local machine, remember to upload the file to Posit cloud first, if you’re using it.
If you know the path online to a file in one of the formats above, you can simply add the full path as the filename within quotation marks, e.g. read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis_data/main/nobel/laureates_df.csv'). For files on GitHub, make sure you use the raw version of the file (click the ‘Raw’ button on the file’s page and copy that address) - the normal GitHub page is a web page, not a csv file.








Warning



If you do want to use your own dataset, be aware that your account on Posit Cloud has a limit of 1GB of RAM. This means that you will not be able to load larger datasets into memory, and you’ll get an error. In this case, it’s best to install R and RStudio on your own machine, which likely has more RAM. Datasets below which are likely to be too big for Posit Cloud are marked (large).

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Datasets used on the course
The datasets we’ve worked with in class are relatively clean and simple, by humanities data standards. For Assignment 1 especially, I highly recommend using one of these: data cleaning and figuring out formats can be very time consuming, so unless you are very comfortable with these things, think carefully before choosing a bespoke dataset.

The Titanic dataset. There are many versions of this on the internet, because it is widely used in machine learning problems. I created a version based on this dataset, because it contains the full list and hasn’t been divided into different parts for training and testing machine learning algorithms. There is a little information on how the dataset was constructed, but unfortunately the link to further information is no longer working. My version is available here.
The Bellevue Almshouse data. Records of immigrants who were admitted to the Bellevue Almshouse (house for the poor) in New York in the 1840s. You can find more information and links to the data here.
The Movie Dialogue dataset. You can find more information about this dataset here. I created the third file, imdb_genre, from a larger IMDB dataset. You can find that file here.
The Nobel Prize Winners dataset. Two tables, with information on the Nobel Prizes and the Nobel Prize winners. I created this using the official Nobel API. You can find the files here.

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Suggested datasets
If you’d like to try something different, the datasets below are similar in spirit to the ones we’ve used in class: tabular, reasonably clean, documented, and about culture or history. Each comes with an idea of the kind of question you could ask of it, but these are just starting points.
When choosing, keep to something broadly humanities-related (so not primarily natural sciences or economics), and check before you commit that there is documentation telling you where the data came from and how it was made - you’ll need it to write a good report.

Good for a first visualisation (Assignment 1)

Art history textbooks (TidyTuesday). Every artist who appears in the two most widely used art history survey textbooks (Janson’s and Gardner’s) across all their editions, with the artists’ gender, ethnicity, nationality, and how much page space each one received. A very direct way into questions about the canon: who gets included, and how has that changed over time? Comes from the R package arthistory.
Eurovision (TidyTuesday). Results of every Eurovision Song Contest, plus the votes cast between countries. Good for rankings over time, and the voting table invites questions about ‘bloc voting’ and which countries favour which (there’s even a mapping project hiding in there).
Bob Ross paintings (TidyTuesday). Every painting from the TV show The Joy of Painting, with the colours used in each one, by season and episode. Small, friendly, and nice for experimenting with colour scales - you can use the actual hex codes of the paints.
Billboard Hot 100 (TidyTuesday). Weekly positions of every song on the US Billboard chart since 1958, joined to Spotify’s audio features (danceability, tempo, and so on). Has songs got shorter, sadder, or faster? A good chance to practise dates and joins.
The Tate collection. Metadata for around 70,000 artworks and 3,500 artists in the Tate’s collection: titles, dates, media, dimensions, acquisition year, and artists’ birth and death places. It’s a 2014 snapshot and no longer updated (which is worth mentioning in your report!), but it is clean and well structured.
The Museum of Modern Art collection. Similar to the Tate data but bigger and regularly updated: artworks with dates, departments, dimensions and acquisition dates, plus artists’ nationality, gender and birth/death years. FiveThirtyEight’s guide to MoMA’s paintings gives a sense of what’s possible.
Post45 Data Collective. Peer-reviewed datasets about twentieth- and twenty-first-century literature, each with a short essay explaining how it was made. Good choices are the New York Times hardcover fiction bestsellers (1931-2020), the index of major literary prizes in the US, and the British literary prizes dataset. Questions about gender, genre and prestige come out of these very naturally.
Project Gutenberg metadata, via the R package gutenbergr. Metadata (not text) for the tens of thousands of books on Project Gutenberg: title, author, authors’ birth and death years, language and subject headings, loaded with gutenberg_metadata, gutenberg_authors and gutenberg_subjects. What does the ‘public domain canon’ look like?



Good for a map (Assignment 2)

Shakespeare and Company Project. Records from Sylvia Beach’s lending library in interwar Paris, with geocoded addresses for its members. An article describes the data, which is divided into members, books, and events (mostly library loans). Map where readers lived, or join the tables to see who borrowed what.
Rijksmonumentenregister. The Dutch register of national monuments - around 60,000 protected buildings and sites, with their type, building period and location. A good local option: map monuments by type or era in Leiden or your home town. Bulk downloads are available via data.overheid.nl (search for ‘rijksmonumenten’).
Dutch-Asiatic Shipping (Huygens Institute). Around 8,000 voyages made by VOC ships between the Netherlands and Asia, 1595-1795, with ships, dates, ports of departure and arrival, and crew numbers. Good for maps of routes and for time series.
Pantheon. Tens of thousands of ‘famous’ historical people, with birthplaces (including coordinates), occupations and a measure of how much their Wikipedia pages are viewed. Fun to map, but also an excellent dataset to be critical about: what does ‘famous’ mean, and whose fame does Wikipedia record?
A cross-verified database of notable people (Laouenan et al., 2022) (large). Around 2.3 million notable people from 3500 BC to 2018, assembled from Wikipedia and Wikidata, with birth and death dates and places, gender and occupation. Much bigger and more systematic than Pantheon; filter it down to a period or region that interests you.
Pleiades. A gazetteer of tens of thousands of places in the ancient world, with coordinates, place types and the periods in which they were in use. Download the CSV ‘dumps’. Good for anyone interested in classics or archaeology.
Mapping Inequality. Digitised versions of the 1930s US government ‘redlining’ maps, which graded neighbourhoods by supposed mortgage risk, largely along racial lines. Downloadable as GeoJSON, so you can practise with polygons rather than points.
The World Atlas of Language Structures, based on WALS. Linguistic features of the world’s languages, with coordinates. It’s a little difficult to find what you need, but the languages table is the most important. Pair it with this dataset of endangered and extinct languages.



More ambitious
These are bigger, messier, or need more care, but reward the effort if you’re feeling confident.

SlaveVoyages. The Trans-Atlantic and Intra-American slave trade databases: records of around 36,000 voyages, with ports, dates, and numbers of enslaved people embarked and disembarked. One of the most important datasets in digital history, and one which demands careful thought about how to visualise human suffering.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access (large). Around half a million objects from the Met’s collection in one CSV, covering everything from ancient Egypt to modern design. Lots of missing values and inconsistencies, which is realistic and makes for good discussion in a report.
Old Bailey Online and the Digital Panopticon. Nearly 200,000 criminal trials at London’s central criminal court, 1674-1913, and the later lives of convicts. Getting tabular data out takes some work; Sharon Howard’s blog posts show how, with R and tidyverse code.
British Library newspapers title list. Every newspaper title held by the British Library, with places and dates of publication. Good for mapping the growth of the press.
litRiddle. Data from a large Dutch reader survey about contemporary novels, combined with information about the books and authors. There’s also an R package: install.packages("litRiddle").
IMDb non-commercial datasets (large). Every film and TV title on IMDb, with genres, runtimes, ratings and cast and crew.
HathiTrust Hathifiles (large). Catalogue metadata (not content) for the millions of volumes digitised by HathiTrust. Look for the most recent file starting with hathi_full.

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Data repositories and lists
There are many, many sources of datasets available online. Look for relatively simple csv and tsv files or sets of files, and avoid those that mention APIs or Linked Open Data unless you are comfortable working with these things.

National and international statistics

CBS Statline: Dutch statistics. Also an R package, cbsodataR.
Eurostat: official EU statistics, at different regional levels - including cultural statistics such as cultural employment and participation.
e-Stat: official statistics repository of Japan. The statistics dashboard is particularly useful.



Humanities repositories

Journal of Open Humanities Data. Short articles describing humanities datasets, with the data attached and possible use cases. A great place to find well-documented data.
Post45 Data Collective (see above).
TidyTuesday. A weekly data challenge with a large archive of datasets, organised by year and week. Many aren’t relevant to the humanities, but those that are tend to be clean and documented.
DANS Social Sciences and Humanities: the Dutch national repository. Lots of datasets, but they can be very specific and not always easy to use.
KB Labs datasets from the Dutch national library (many are text-based but some are structured).
The Pudding has some nice and often fun datasets, though they have a very American focus.
Melanie Walsh’s Introduction to Cultural Analytics has a page of datasets. Not all are tabular - some are primarily text, which is outside the scope of this course.
The Google dataset search. However, make sure you can trace back the provenance!
The ‘DH toychest’ datasets and this list of museum APIs. Both are old, so expect some broken links, but there are still useful things there.







Tip



For very large datasets, it may also be helpful to use an R package such as data.table which is more efficient than Tidyverse for working with very large data. data.table has a very different syntax to the Tidyverse, but there is a package, tidytable, which converts between the two.

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
R packages
There are many R ‘dataset packages’. These can be very useful, because accessing the data is simple - you just need to install a package and then follow some instructions to load the dataset, rather than find and upload a spreadsheet file. They are also generally formatted so they are easy to use in R.

HistData: classic datasets from the history of data visualisation - including Florence Nightingale’s data on causes of death in the Crimean War, John Snow’s cholera map, and Minard’s data on Napoleon’s march on Moscow. You could recreate (and improve on?) a famous chart.
arthistory: the art history textbook data described above.
gutenbergr: Project Gutenberg metadata (see above).
taylor: the complete discography of Taylor Swift, with Spotify audio features and lyrics. See the package website.
refugees: UNHCR data on refugees and displaced people, from 1951 onwards.
A huge list of datasets in R packages here - but again, try to only use those with good documentation.


R packages which connect to an API

The osmdata package. Download geographic data from OpenStreetMap through R. Very fun to work with, though takes some understanding of the queries. Try a tutorial here if you’re interested.
spotifyr allows you to download data from Spotify. You need to register for an API key. Be aware that since late 2024 Spotify no longer gives new apps access to its ‘audio features’ (danceability, energy and so on), so much of what you’ll see in older tutorials won’t work. Datasets which already include these features, such as the Billboard data above, are a better bet.

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Social media data
Unfortunately, doing analysis on social media data has become very difficult in the last few years as companies have locked down their services. Twitter/X ended free and academic access to its API in 2023, which means older collections of tweet IDs can no longer be ‘hydrated’ into actual tweets, and Reddit has also heavily restricted access. Unless you have a ready-made, documented dataset (and permission to use it), I’d avoid social media data for this course.

title: 56  Data and Inspiration
text:
Inspiration for your reports

Current Research in Digital History (short historical essays with graphics).
Journal of Digital History (digital history articles with a code layer).
Journal of Cultural Analytics (computational articles on culture, often with visual elements).
The Pudding (data journalism visual essays with interactive elements).
Visualizing Emancipation (a nice example of a visual essay aimed at an academic readership).
The Killing Times (example of an interactive visual essay, for those interested in using Shiny).
Short visual essays by FiveThirtyEight such as this one, and their guide to MoMA’s paintings, which is a nice example of the kind of project you could make with collections data.
Sharon Howard’s data blogs. Some use other tech, but many are straightforward R/tidyverse visualisations with historical data, such as here.
The Programming Historian (peer-reviewed tutorials, several of which use R and historical data).
Cool stuff made with cultural heritage APIs.

title: 57  Preparing for the Exam
text:
How to prepare

Do the home exercises. Only two are graded, but they are all written to prepare you for this exam and for the reports. Reading code is much easier once you’ve written lots of it.
Use the ‘Check your understanding’ boxes at the end of chapters. They are written in the same style as Part A and B questions. Where there’s a code cell, predict the answer first, and then run the code to check.
Go through the Learning Objectives at the end of each chapter. If you can’t tick one off, go back over that chapter.
Practise critiquing. Whenever you see a chart in the news or on social media, ask yourself what it does well and what you’d change. The chapters on Gestalt principles, colour, and accessibility give you the vocabulary.

title: 57  Preparing for the Exam
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Data analysis (weeks 1-2)

Explain what a dataframe is, and what rows, columns and data types are
Predict the output of select(), slice(), arrange(), filter(), mutate(), count(), group_by() and summarise()
Follow a chain of functions joined with the pipe (|>), step by step
Explain what a join does, what a key is, and why a left_join() can produce NA values
Explain the difference between ‘wide’ and ‘long’ (tidy) data
Spot common mistakes, such as = instead of ==, or forgetting quotation marks



Data visualisation (weeks 3-4)

Explain how ggplot2 maps columns of data to aesthetics (x, y, colour, fill, size…) using aes()
Explain the difference between setting an aesthetic inside and outside aes()
Choose an appropriate chart type (geom) for a given question and type of data
Explain what scales do, and when to use a sequential, diverging, or qualitative colour scale
Use Gestalt principles to explain why a chart works, or doesn’t
Explain the role of titles, labels and annotations in telling a story with data



Ethics, FAIR data and accessibility (week 5)

Explain the FAIR principles and evaluate a dataset against them
Identify accessibility problems in a visualisation (e.g. colour-blindness, contrast, missing alt text) and suggest fixes
Discuss how a dataset or visualisation was made, and whose perspective it represents
Explain how choices such as filtering, scales, titles and the handling of missing values can make a visualisation misleading
Suggest more respectful ways to visualise sensitive topics



Digital mapping (weeks 5-6)

Explain what a simple features (sf) object is, and how it differs from a regular dataframe
Explain the steps of joining a dataset to a map, and spot problems with a join
Explain how to turn a dataset of coordinates into points on a map
Explain what a map projection is, and how the choice of projection can distort a map
Explain when to use a choropleth and when to use a points map
Explain why choropleth maps usually need normalised data (e.g. per person) rather than raw counts

title: 57  Preparing for the Exam
text:
Function reference sheet
This is the reference sheet you’ll be given in the exam.

Function reference sheet






Function
What it does




select(df, col1, col2)
Keep only the named columns. select(df, -col1) removes a column.


slice(df, 1:5)
Keep rows by position. slice_max(df, col, n = 5) / slice_min() keep the rows with the highest/lowest values.


arrange(df, col)
Sort rows by a column, smallest first. arrange(df, desc(col)) sorts largest first.


filter(df, condition)
Keep rows where the condition is TRUE. Comparisons: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=, %in%. Combine with & (and), | (or); negate with !.


str_detect(col, "text")
TRUE if the text is found in the column (often used inside filter()).


mutate(df, new_col = ...)
Add a new column, or change an existing one.


if_else(condition, yes, no)
Return one value if a condition is TRUE, another if FALSE. case_when() handles several conditions.


rename(df, new_name = old_name)
Rename a column.


count(df, col)
Count the number of rows for each value of a column.


group_by(df, col)
Group rows, so that the next function is applied to each group separately.


summarise(df, new_col = ...)
Reduce each group to one row, e.g. with n(), sum(), mean(), max(), min().


left_join(x, y, by = "key")
Add the columns of y to x, matching rows by a key. Keeps all rows of x; rows with no match get NA. Also inner_join(), full_join().


pivot_longer() / pivot_wider()
Reshape data from wide to long format, or from long to wide.


ggplot(df, aes(x = , y = , colour = , fill = , size = ))
Start a chart, mapping columns to aesthetics.


geom_point(), geom_line(), geom_col(), geom_bar(), geom_histogram(), geom_text()
Draw the data as points, lines, bars, a histogram, or text.


scale_x_continuous(), scale_x_date(), scale_fill_brewer(), scale_colour_viridis_d(), …
Control how data values are translated into positions or colours.


facet_wrap(~ col)
Split a chart into small multiples, one per value of a column.


labs(title = , x = , y = , caption = )
Set titles and labels.


annotate()
Add a single piece of text or a shape to a chart.


theme_minimal(), theme()
Change the overall look of the chart.


geom_sf()
Draw an sf object (a map): polygons, lines or points. Positions come from the geometry column.


coord_sf(xlim = , ylim = , crs = )
Zoom in on a map, and/or change its projection.


st_read()
Read a map file (e.g. a GeoJSON file or shapefile) into an sf object.


st_as_sf(df, coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'), crs = 4326)
Turn a dataframe with coordinates into an sf object of points.


separate_rows(df, col, sep = ', ')
Split a column containing several values into separate rows.

A1. What is the output of this code? Write out the resulting table.
books |>
  filter(year > 1700, format == "octavo") |>
  select(title, pages)






Answer

Robinson Crusoe

Only two rows have a year after 1700 and the format octavo (Pamela is after 1700 but is a duodecimo; Pilgrim’s Progress is an octavo but before 1700). select() then keeps only two columns.



A2. How many rows will the result of this code have, and what will be in the first row?
books |>
  group_by(format) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_pages = mean(pages)) |>
  arrange(desc(n))






Answer





Four rows, one for each format. The first row is octavo, with n = 3 and mean_pages = 298.7 (the average of 232, 364 and 300). summarise() reduces each group to a single row, and arrange(desc(n)) puts the most common format first.



A3. A student wants to count how many of the books were published in each century. Which of these will work?

books |> count(year)
books |> mutate(century = if_else(year < 1700, "17th", "18th")) |> count(century)
books |> filter(year < 1700) |> count(year)
books |> group_by(year < 1700)







Answer





b. It first makes a new column, century, and then counts the values in it (3 and 3). (a) counts each individual year, giving six rows with a count of 1. (c) only looks at the 17th century, and again counts individual years. (d) groups the data, but doesn’t count anything.



A4. What does this code produce for Pilgrim’s Progress, and why?
books |>
  left_join(authors, by = "author") |>
  mutate(age = year - born) |>
  select(author, age)






Answer





NA. Bunyan isn’t in the authors table, so the left_join() keeps the row (because books is on the left) but has no value to put in the born column, so it puts NA. Any calculation with NA also gives NA. The other rows give the author’s age when the book was published (e.g. 63 for Hobbes).



A5. What does this return?
books |>
  arrange(desc(pages)) |>
  slice(1:2)






Answer





The two longest books: Leviathan (396 pages) and Robinson Crusoe (364 pages), with all their columns. arrange(desc(pages)) sorts the longest first, and slice(1:2) keeps the first two rows. slice_max(books, pages, n = 2) would do the same thing in one step.



A6. This code gives an error. What’s wrong, and how would you fix it?
books |>
  filter(format = "quarto")






Answer





A single = is used to set a value (e.g. an argument to a function), not to compare. To test whether two things are equal, you need ==: filter(format == "quarto").





Part B: Code and charts (20%)
B1. Which of these produces a scatterplot of year against number of pages, with the points coloured by format? For each of the others, explain what goes wrong.

ggplot(books, aes(x = year, y = pages, colour = format)) + geom_point()
ggplot(books, aes(x = year, y = pages)) + geom_point(colour = format)
ggplot(books, aes(x = year, y = pages, fill = format)) + geom_point()
ggplot(books, aes(x = format, y = pages)) + geom_col()







Answer





a. In (b), colour = format is outside aes(), so R doesn’t look for a column called format in the data - it gives an error. In (c), the points are drawn with fill mapped to format, but the default points are solid dots that have no fill, only a colour, so they all appear black. (d) is a bar chart of the total number of pages for each format, not a scatterplot.



B2. A student writes the following code, expecting blue points. Instead the points are a pinkish-red, and there’s a legend with the single entry ‘blue’. Why, and how would you fix it?
ggplot(books, aes(x = year, y = pages)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))






Answer





Inside aes(), ggplot treats "blue" as a data value (as if there was a column where every row said “blue”), not as a colour. It gives that value the first colour in its default palette, and adds a legend for it. To set a fixed colour, put it outside aes(): geom_point(colour = "blue").



B3. You’ve made a line chart of the number of books published per year, with one line per format. The lines overlap so much that it’s hard to read. Name two different changes you could make to the code to improve it, and explain what each does.






Answer





Good answers include:

facet_wrap(~ format) to give each format its own small panel (small multiples), so the lines no longer overlap.
Highlight one format and make the others grey, to focus on the story you want to tell.
Label the lines directly (e.g. with geom_text() or annotate()) instead of using a legend.
Summarise by decade instead of year (using mutate() and group_by()), to make the lines smoother.






Part C: Critique a visualisation (25%)
C1. This chart shows the proportion of passengers who survived the sinking of the Titanic, by ticket class. Identify at least four problems with it, and explain how you would fix each.







Answer






The y-axis doesn’t start at zero. Bar charts encode values by the length of the bar, so a truncated axis exaggerates the differences: the first-class bar looks about six times as long as the third-class bar, when the real difference is about 2.5 times. Start the axis at zero.
The colours carry no information and are hard to read. Red, green and blue are just repeating the x-axis, and red/green is a problem for colour-blind readers. Use a single colour, or a sequential palette if you want to emphasise the ordering of the classes.
The legend is redundant, and its title (‘factor(pclass)’) is a leftover from the code. Remove it.
The axis labels are column names, not explanations. Use e.g. ‘Ticket class’ (with labels ‘First’, ‘Second’, ‘Third’) and ‘Share of passengers who survived’, ideally as a percentage.
The title is sensationalist, and doesn’t tell the reader what they’re looking at. A good title states the finding plainly, e.g. ‘First-class passengers were more than twice as likely to survive as those in third class’.
The dark background reduces contrast. Use a light theme such as theme_minimal().
No source is given. Add a caption.




C2. This map was made for a report arguing that Germany, France, and the UK are Europe’s most ‘bookish’ countries. The fill colour shows each country’s total population. Identify the problems with the map, and with the way it’s being used.







Answer






The data doesn’t match the claim. The map shows total population, not reading. Big countries will always look ‘more’ of everything on a map of raw counts. To say anything about reading, you would need data about reading (e.g. library loans, book sales), and you’d need to normalise it - e.g. loans per person - so that countries of different sizes can be compared.
The rainbow colour scale has no natural order (is pink more than blue?), creates false boundaries between colours, and is not colour-blind friendly. For ordered numeric data, use a sequential palette (e.g. light to dark of one hue, or viridis).
The legend is unreadable: its title is a column name (pop_est) and the numbers are in scientific notation (8e+07). Give it a proper title (‘Population (millions)’) and readable labels.
The title makes a claim which the map can’t support.
No source is given, and there’s no information about the year of the data.
The projection: this map uses plain longitude and latitude, which stretches countries further from the equator (compare the size of Scandinavia and Spain). A projection designed for Europe would be better.






Part D: Plan an analysis (25%)
D1. You’re given a (simplified) dataset of voyages made by ships of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) from the Netherlands to Asia between 1595 and 1795. Each row is one voyage, with these columns:

ship_name: the name of the ship
departure_date: the date the ship left the Netherlands
departure_port: the Dutch port it left from
arrival_date: the date it arrived in Asia (empty if it never arrived)
arrival_port: the port it arrived at in Asia
crew_departure: the number of people on board when it left
crew_arrival: the number of people on board when it arrived

Your research question is: How did the deadliness of the voyage to Asia change over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries?
Explain, step by step, how you would use this data to answer the question. Mention the functions you would use, and the chart you would make (and why). Then discuss at least two problems or limitations with the data, or ethical issues, that you would need to consider in your report.






Answer





A strong answer would include something like the following. You don’t need to write perfect code: a clear explanation in words, naming the relevant functions, is enough.
Steps:

filter() to keep only voyages which arrived, and where both crew columns have values (and explain that you’ve done this - see the problems below).
mutate() to calculate the number of deaths (crew_departure - crew_arrival) and, more importantly, the proportion who died (deaths / crew_departure). The proportion is better than the raw number, because ships became bigger over time, so a raw count would mostly show the size of the ships.
mutate() to extract the year from departure_date, and then make a decade column (e.g. floor(year / 10) * 10).
group_by(decade) and summarise() to calculate the average proportion of deaths per decade, and the number of voyages, n().
Make a line chart (geom_line()) with decade on the x-axis and the average mortality on the y-axis, because the question is about change over time. Add clear labels, a title that states the finding, a source, and perhaps annotations for important events.

Problems and limitations (any two, well explained):

Missing data: ships which were wrecked or captured never arrived, so they have no arrival crew number. If you filter them out, you leave out the most deadly voyages, and underestimate mortality. You could count these separately, or make a second chart of the share of ships that never arrived.
The numbers don’t only reflect deaths: people could also leave or join the ship at stops along the way (e.g. at the Cape), so a lower number on arrival isn’t only deaths.
Sources and FAIR: you’d need to find out where the numbers come from (VOC records), how they were transcribed, and how complete they are for different periods - the early decades may be less well recorded.
Ethics and perspective: this data was produced by a colonial trading company, and records people as numbers of ‘crew’. It says nothing about who they were, and nothing about the people in Asia affected by the VOC. You could reflect on whose perspective the data represents, and on how to present deaths respectfully (e.g. avoiding sensationalist titles).
